note.text: An earthquake is shaking caused by a sudden release of energy, commonly involving movement on a fault. The focus is the origin within Earth; the epicentre is directly above it on the surface. Effects include ground shaking and possible damage, landslides or other secondary hazards depending on the setting. Magnitude measures event size; intensity describes observed effects at a place. Preparedness and safer buildings can reduce losses. A school lesson cannot predict the precise time of the next damaging earthquake.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: An earthquake is shaking caused by a sudden release of energy, commonly involving movement on a fault. The focus is the origin within Earth; the epicentre is directly above it on the surface. Effects include ground shaking and possible damage, landslides or other secondary hazards depending on the setting. Magnitude measures event size; intensity describes observed effects at a place. Preparedness and safer buildings can reduce losses. A school lesson cannot predict the precise time of the next damaging earthquake.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: A classroom can practise recognised protective actions before an event. If indoors when shaking begins, drop, cover your head and neck under a nearby sturdy table where possible, and hold on; stay clear of windows. Do not rush down stairs during shaking. Actual emergency instructions must be adapted by responsible local authorities to the building and setting.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Distinguish the cause, the location terms and the measured effects. Do not say that a single magnitude gives identical damage everywhere: distance, ground and buildings matter. Practise the school's plan with an adult. During a real emergency, follow responsible local instructions and trained responders.
